Title: Agent incident playbooks
Description: Writing incident playbooks for three agent scenarios: the agent is wrong (it acted on a false conclusion, closed real alerts, changed the wrong thing); the agent is stopped (its identity expired, the provider is down, it ran out of compute) and its work must continue by hand; the agent is compromised (an attacker steered it through content it read). Plans name who can stop the agent (NCSC)

Title: Ways to stop an agent
Description: The ways to stop an agent and when to use each: revoke its identity or session token so it can no longer call any tool; disable only the tools or connectors it misuses while the rest keeps running; put it in observe-only mode, where it may analyse and recommend but is barred from acting; roll back what it changed using its action log

Title: Investigating a compromised agent
Description: Where the attack comes from: content the agent reads (logs, alerts, tickets, documents, emails, web pages) can carry instructions aimed at it, so the investigator looks for injection in those sources and cuts any that is poisoned. What the agent did: knowing, for each of the bank's agents, which records exist that the agent cannot write to and how to pull them fast (the platform's audit log of tool calls with arguments and times, gateway and network logs, logs of the systems it touched), then building the timeline from them, because a compromised agent's own summary can omit or misstate what it did

Title: Cleaning up
Description: Cleaning up after a manipulated agent: finding the injected content it acted on and removing it from the sources the agent reads; clearing anything it stored in its memory as a result; re-running the same injection against the agent before putting it back in service

Title: Operating without the agent
Description: The manual fallback for what the agent handled (triage queue, enrichment, first response), the staffing to sustain it for days, and the regular drill that proves it still works

Title: Reporting
Description: What regulators expect in an incident report when an agent caused or worsened the incident (DORA, HKMA, MAS), and which evidence to preserve for it

Title: Recording the AI step
Description: Recording any AI step applied to evidence so it can be repeated and defended: the tool, model and version, the exact prompt and settings, the output, and who verified it. The original artefact stays the evidence; AI output is a derived analysis, never a substitute

Title: Forensic readiness for agents
Description: Defining what every agent must log (prompt and response, each tool call with its arguments, data retrieved, memory writes, approvals given), stored where the agent cannot alter it, time-synchronised and integrity-protected, retained long enough for an investigation (vendors default to 7 to 30 days), and tested by reconstructing a past incident from it

Title: Investigating an agent as suspect
Description: Rebuilding the agent's actions from its traces, finding the input that steered it, and attributing each action to the human it acted for or to the attacker

Title: AI attack classes
Description: Direct prompt injection; indirect injection through content the agent reads (documents, web pages, tool results, emails); jailbreaks and guardrail evasion; data exfiltration through the agent's own tools; making the agent exceed its intended authority; tool poisoning (a malicious tool description) and rug pulls (a tool that changes after it was approved)

Title: Published methods
Description: The OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide, the Cloud Security Alliance's Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide (12 categories) and MITRE ATLAS techniques

Title: Attacks across agents
Description: Compromising one agent to steer others, injecting into an orchestrator's plan, tampering with messages between agents

Title: Attacks on model and platform
Description: Extracting the model or its instructions, poisoning the agent's memory, escaping the sandbox, timing side channels

Title: Automated red-team programme
Description: Building and running automated red-team harnesses (PyRIT-class tooling) and a continuous programme that re-tests every agent when its model, tools or prompts change

Title: Containment before a run
Description: A network segment from which the agent can reach only in-scope targets; egress allow-lists verified by test, not assumed; a fresh sandbox per run; credentials scoped to the engagement and expiring with it

Title: Monitoring during a run
Description: Watching the agent's actions out of band (not its reports); a named person with the authority and the means to kill the run within minutes; the triggers for doing so (an action outside scope, contact with a third party, a credential used elsewhere)

Title: Escape patterns
Description: The escape patterns seen in practice: attacking something else when the assigned target proves impossible, reading an ambiguous message as approval, creating accounts or identities, carrying on after the window closes, contacting real people

Title: Trajectory-level validation
Description: Validating findings from the transcript, not the summary: check that the evidence the agent cites exists (a 'successful login' that was a redirect, credentials that do not work), reproduce the exploit by hand before reporting, and treat the agent's self-assessment as untrusted

Title: Collateral findings
Description: A disclosure lane for what to do when the agent finds something outside the engagement

Title: Discovery
Description: Finding every MCP server and agent connector in the estate, including those developers run on their own workstations, by searching configuration files and by recognising the MCP protocol in network traffic

Title: Inventory
Description: For each agent and tool server: its owner, version, the tools it exposes, the permissions it holds, the systems it reaches, and the guardrails around it

Title: Content-bound approval
Description: Approving a tool by the hash of its description and code, and checking each session that it has not been silently redefined since (the rug pull)

Title: Scanning
Description: Running MCP and Skill scanners in the build pipeline and on a schedule for tool poisoning, instructions hidden in tool descriptions, servers exposed without authentication and credentials stored in plain text

Title: AI bill of materials
Description: A bill of materials for AI components: which models, tools and Skills a system uses and where each came from

Title: Vetting third parties
Description: Vetting third-party Skills and connectors before they are allowed in

Title: Why set-up is the skill
Description: The same model finds under a tenth or over half of the vulnerabilities in a codebase depending on how it is given context and driven, and filters a third or almost all of a static analyser's false positives for the same reason

Title: Giving the model context
Description: Supplying the functions a target calls, type definitions, the data-flow path to the input and build information, using static and dynamic analysis tools to supply that context automatically

Title: Framework, model and method
Description: Choosing the agent framework and the model for the task, and driving the model through a structured method rather than letting it explore freely

Title: Confirming before reporting
Description: A proof of vulnerability (an input or exploit that demonstrates it in a sandbox), the same test against the patched and unpatched versions, and several runs with a majority verdict

Title: Reliability by vulnerability class
Description: Which classes models find well (memory safety, anything a fuzzer can reach) and which they over-report (documented behaviour reported as a bug, inflated severity, duplicates), and setting thresholds per class

Title: Deduplication and cost
Description: Removing duplicates (by stack trace or sanitiser signature) and keeping cost under control at scale

Title: Measuring the harness
Description: Measuring the harness on a corpus of known vulnerabilities before trusting it

Title: Classifying agent actions
Description: For each action an agent can take in a process (a payment, a data deletion, an email to a client, a firewall change), rating its impact and whether it can be undone, and assigning a tier: autonomous, autonomous with logging, human approval, two-person approval, prohibited

Title: Enforcement outside the model
Description: An authorisation point between the agent's plan and its execution that checks every action against its tier and the agent's permissions, so the decision never depends on the model obeying its instructions

Title: The stop mechanism
Description: No standard defines a kill switch, so it is designed as a set of levers (interrupt the task, revoke credentials, cut tool access, quarantine the agent, roll back its changes), each with who may trigger it, how fast it takes effect and how it is tested

Title: The audit trail
Description: What is recorded (reasoning artefacts, each tool call with its arguments, data accessed, messages between agents, approvals), where (a store the agent cannot write to), for how long, and how each action is tied to the person the agent acted for

Title: The oversight interface
Description: How an approval request is shown so a person can judge it (what will happen, in plain language, with the risk and the agent's confidence), limiting the volume of requests so approvers do not click through them, and what overseers must be trained on

Title: Reference architectures
Description: Reference architectures for the bank's agent platforms and how the above is implemented on each

Title: Agent control catalogue
Description: The control catalogue for agents and how to test each control: a distinct identity and permissions per agent, tool allow-lists, logging that the agent cannot alter, approval gates for high-impact actions, change control on prompts, tools and models

Title: Assuring assurance's own AI
Description: Documenting, validating and monitoring the AI used to produce assessments and gather evidence

Title: Registering an agent
Description: Its own identity (never a shared or human credential), a human sponsor recorded in the directory who is accountable for it, a stated purpose and a declared list of what it may do

Title: Delegated authority
Description: Issuing and reading tokens in which the subject is the person and the actor is the agent (token exchange, on-behalf-of flows), with the person's consent recorded, and what the agent may then do in that person's name

Title: Connector and MCP scopes
Description: Reading what a scope actually permits in the bank's applications and tool servers, granting the minimum, and reviewing grants

Title: Just-in-time access
Description: Privilege granted for a task and a time window with no standing privilege, and the conditions that require a human to approve the grant

Title: Short-lived sub-agents
Description: Identities that exist for seconds, with a time to live and no more rights than the parent

Title: Recertification
Description: Quarterly for agents and monthly for high-privilege ones, with de-provisioning triggered when the sponsor leaves or the purpose lapses

Title: Revocation drills
Description: Revoking an agent's identity and its live sessions within minutes, and verifying that it worked

Title: Integration with IGA, PAM, SIEM
Description: Integrating the agent authorisation point with identity governance, privileged access and the SIEM: registration, scoped issuance, just-in-time grants, recertification and revocation signals flowing between them

Title: Privileged access and break-glass
Description: Privileged access and break-glass for agents inside the existing privileged-access model

Title: Audit trail and standards
Description: The audit trail regulators ask for (which agent, on whose behalf, which tools, what data, what reasoning) and the standards still being written (IETF agent identity, OpenID AuthZEN, MCP authorisation), so the design does not lock into one vendor's delegation model
